comments.text:
Some things I dont agree with. Many things and misconceptions caused because the HDR on Windows is just too buggy and require so many steps to activate it as intended. I recently swapped my laptop panel with a mini-led 1200 nit peak-brightness HDR panel. So SDR content on a HDR monitor is not supposed to look washed out (I believe this caused by color profile's wrong gamma management). I had the same issue in the beginning "washed out SDR" and almost accepted that I should only turn it on when I will watch or play HDR content. Wasnt necessary after doing some tweaks. Now my desktop and SDR content still looks vivid when HDR turned on.

-Uninstalled both GPU drivers with DDU, Uninstalled Armory Crate (Has Game Visual managing screen color profile on ASUS products)
-Removed all color profiles from Color Management in Control Panel (I believe this has fixed the issue for me as I believe Windows Color Management is buggy too)
-Installed new GPU drivers with clean installation, installed Armory Crate
-I needed my Panel's ICM profile since my laptop doesnt come with this panel originally (but it is present in newer Asus models) so Armory crate cant download and apply it. Someone on GitHub shared his laptop's GameVisual folder so I grabbed the files from there. There are only 4 files you need and to understand which one is which you look at the file name. It will have laptop model, followed by a number or number letter combination which is actually GPU brand's hardware ID, and followed by panel's EDID. I found the 4 files (2 for my intel gpu that has my panel's EDID, 2 for my Nvidia gpu with my panel's EDID) and renamed the file with my laptop's model number so Armory Crate can see and use the file. So gamevisual started working correctly.
-Make sure you turn off "Change brightness based on content" in Windows settings as it bugs with HDR sometimes and make your screen lot more dimm when you activate HDR
-I activated HDR, made sure the brightness and HDR content brightness slider is to the max. This is important otherwise you wont be able to do HDR calibration correctly. 
-Started windows HDR calibration and Saved the profile. (Ive done it for both my GPU's so I have 2 different calibration file)


And hopefully these should make it work for you too.

comments.text:
I went through a lot of trial and error with HDR, so here are some additional recommendations to save you the trouble: that weren’t covered in the video:
1. Windows HDR Calibration app limitations
The Windows HDR Calibration app can be misleading. For example, on a Samsung Odyssey Neo G7 (with a measured peak brightness of ~1200–1300 nits for a 10% window, per Monitors Unboxed), following the square test often results in a value around ~850 nits. This is inaccurate.
Additionally, the app may suggest similar values for both peak brightness (small window) and full-frame brightness, which is not technically correct—these values should differ due to panel behavior (ABL, etc.).
Recommendation: Do not strictly rely on the square test. Instead, refer to trusted measurements (e.g., RTINGS, Monitors Unboxed) and input those values manually for more accurate calibration. UPD: This was covered in the video:)

2. Check panel-reported luminance (dxdiag)
You can export a dxdiag report and review the luminance-related values. Some OLED and Mini-LED displays already come reasonably well-calibrated at the firmware level, which can provide a more reliable baseline than the Windows tool.

3. Game-level HDR calibration matters more
Many modern AAA games (e.g., Cyberpunk, The Last of Us, Resident Evil) use their own HDR pipelines and bypass Windows HDR calibration settings.
Recommendation: Always perform HDR calibration within each game’s settings menu, as those values will take precedence over the system-level configuration. UPD: This was also covered in the video:)

4. By default, NVIDIA may use an 8-bit color depth and limited dynamic range, which is not suitable for proper HDR.
Before configuring HDR, go to the NVIDIA Control Panel (or NVIDIA App) and set:
Output color depth: 10-bit (or higher, if available)
Output dynamic range: Full
Proper HDR requires at least a 10-bit signal path, so ensuring these settings are correct is essential for accurate HDR output.

What you'll also forget is some important things when it comes to windows hdr: Microsoft forces scRGB over the SDR content in short which is wrong and that's why HDR is looking washed out when displaying SDR content inside HDR or when HDR is activated. This is also applicable to the HDR Calibration App which will only effect HDR content mastered in SRGB which most content including sdr content such as the desktop are not. 

Basically the HDR Calibration app is only then useful if you exactly know that the content you display is origianally mastered SRGB or scRGB.

Most content is in gamma 2.2 which makes the calibration app not really reliable because it messes with content which is in HDR10 PQ for example or sdr content with gamma 2.2.

If I am wrong with certain aspects or so please correct me so I get the opportunity to learn and improve my knowledge :)

comments.text:
To my knowlwdge, there's not a single game out there, that uses anything other than sRGB sprites. Sprites are the images, wrapping around 3D models (UV mapping). So, they are using 8-bit images all the way, which is why most games don't look great in HDR.

There is free software out there, that can show you scopes in most games, and will confirm that despite the game being shown in HDR, no color goes outside the sRGB color space. Some of these software can also stretch the sRGB to a wider color space, but in most cases it just doesn't look great, because you are simply stretching 8-bit colors to a wider color space, so you are simply not getting more colors, but essentially just moving those potential 16 million colors to an area, that can support 1 billion.
And 16 million colors sounds like a lot, but any scene of any given time, usually only shows a fraction of those colors.

comments.text: @poke-you-tube  SDR calibration is done to 100 nits, HDR sets paper-white to 203 nits.  The only items in HDR that get set to maximum are any highlights in the image.  It looks bright, but it's not set to maximum.  ZeNeo.X is correct on this.  What you're seeing and confusing with maximum brightness is either a monitor mode setting error OR terrible Auto HDR.  If you go into HDR mode and everything looks overly bright and washed out you either have your monitor set incorrectly or you are trying to wring HDR out of something like an IPS monitor.
